title: Database replication and sharding
summary: Replication for read scaling and failover (leader–follower, replication lag), sharding for write/storage scaling, choosing a shard key, and the hot-shard and cross-shard pitfalls.
note:
1. Replication = copies of the same data
   • Leader takes writes, followers serve reads → scales reads + failover
   • Followers lag → a read right after a write may be stale
2. Sharding = split data across nodes by a shard key
   • Scales writes + storage past one machine
   • Bad key → hot shard; cross-shard queries/joins are expensive
3. Replicate first; shard only when one node can't hold the write/data load
✎ In my words: ______________________________________________

recall.q: What does leader–follower replication scale, and what does it not?
recall.a: It scales reads and gives failover, but not write throughput — all writes still go to the single leader.

recall.q: What is replication lag and when does it bite?
recall.a: Followers apply writes slightly behind the leader; a read-after-write on a follower can return stale data.
A shard key that concentrates traffic (e.g. sharding by date so 'today' gets all writes, or a few huge accounts).

shot.title: Replication vs sharding
shot.body:
| | replication | sharding |
|---|---|---|
| copies | same data N times | different data per node |
| scales | reads, availability | writes, storage |
| risk | stale reads (lag) | hot shard, cross-shard joins |
| when | read-heavy, need HA | one node can't hold load |

sections.title: Replication
sections.body:
✍️ Keep multiple copies of the same dataset. In **leader–follower**, the leader takes all writes and streams them to followers; reads fan out to followers. This scales **reads** and provides **failover** (promote a follower if the leader dies).
✍️ **Multi-leader / leaderless** setups accept writes in more places for availability but must resolve conflicts.

sections.title: Replication lag
sections.body:
✍️ Followers apply changes slightly after the leader, so a read on a follower can miss a just-made write (read-after-write anomaly).
- Fixes: route a user's reads to the leader right after they write, or track a version/timestamp and wait for the follower to catch up.
```java
if (justWrote(userId)) row = leader.read(id); // read-your-writes
else row = follower.read(id);                 // normal, may lag
```

sections.title: Sharding (partitioning)
sections.body: ✍️ Split the dataset across nodes so each holds a slice, keyed by a **shard key** — hash-based (even spread) or range-based (good for range scans). This scales **write throughput** and **storage** beyond one machine, since each shard handles its own writes.

sections.title: Choosing a shard key
sections.body: ✍️ A good key spreads load evenly and keeps related rows together. **Hot shard:** a key that concentrates traffic (sharding by day puts all of today's writes on one shard; a celebrity user overwhelms their shard). **Cross-shard queries/joins** fan out to every shard and are slow — design the key around your dominant access pattern.

sections.title: Do them in order
sections.body: ✍️ Replication is simpler and usually enough; reach for sharding only when a single node can no longer hold the write volume or data size, since sharding adds real operational and query complexity.
